base_latency_ms.measured_context: Google Cloud Storage as an online origin, as operated by Spotify at petabyte scale; per-request latency for a point read, quoted by Spotify's own engineering blog. Band: the 30-100 ms spread is the source's own stated range, not a derived one. It is a general GCS per-request figure, NOT a measurement of Spotify's audio-origin path.

citations.note: 'GCS delivers 30-100ms per request'. Same post: 'At Spotify, petabytes reside in Bigtable for online use-cases - but exabytes sit in the GCS data lake.'

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 9,000 req/s peak. Streaming is modelled as CHUNKED HTTP RANGE REQUESTS, not HLS/DASH segments: Spotify says 'the Spotify app will fetch the file in chunks from a nearby server with HTTP GET range requests. A typical chunk size is 512kB' (Spotify Engineering, 2018-08-31, 'Smoother streaming with BBR'). At the ~128 kbit/s ladder average this file already assumes for BYTES, 512 kB is ~32 s of audio, so ~160,000 concurrent listeners generate ~5,000 chunk GET/s - about 55% of requests - where the old 'one GET per ~10 s of audio' assumption implied ~16,000/s and a 0.80 audio share. The control-plane rates are pinned to the SAME 160,000 listeners and are UNCHANGED in absolute terms; only their share of the total rose, because the audio denominator shrank.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: The v1 engine is an analytical open-queueing model of REQUEST arrivals. It cannot express a long-lived socket, a bitrate ladder, or per-session state. Chunked delivery is the closest honest shape and is what THIS ENGINE CAN EXPRESS - that is the claim, not a claim about what every real player does. It happens to match Spotify's own mechanism (512 kB HTTP GET range requests issued over an already-open connection), so 'one server request per chunk' is a fair arrival process here; a raw-socket progressive-download design would NOT be modelled correctly.

assumptions.subject: cdn
assumptions.statement: CDN hit rate is ASSUMED at 97% on audio chunks, so only 3% of chunk requests reach the origin store. NO Spotify cache-hit-rate figure is public and none is cited here - the 97% is a guess. What IS measured is the popularity concentration the guess rests on: '88% of the track accesses were within the most popular 12% of the library' and, for server-side requests specifically, '79% of accesses being within the most popular 21%' (Kreitz & Niemela, IEEE P2P'10, 2010; the P2P overlay that paper measured was retired in 2014, the popularity distribution is what survives). A hot set that concentrated makes a high edge hit rate plausible; the exact digit is not evidence, and origin load scales linearly with (1 - hit rate).

assumptions.subject: api
assumptions.statement: Control-plane API ~2,000 rps/instance at ~10 ms of service time. NO public Spotify figure exists for either; both are generic app-server assumptions. This tier FRONTS search but does not perform retrieval - ranking happens in the `search` tier - so do not read its capacity as the search budget. About 44% of requests now touch origin compute where the old file said 20%; that is purely the audio denominator shrinking, not extra control-plane load.

assumptions.subject: analytics
assumptions.statement: One play event per playback start, consumed at ~800 events/s per instance (counter updates plus royalty attribution writes)

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The SQL primary is modelled as ONE instance because there is one writer. A Multi-AZ standby is assumed in a real deployment but is NOT modelled as a second instance: it serves no traffic, and the engine would credit it with capacity it does not have. The engine will therefore flag the primary as a single point of failure - that flag is correct about failover, not about capacity.

assumptions.subject: store
assumptions.statement: ~5 PB origin: ~100M tracks ('over 100 million tracks', Spotify newsroom company-info page, which carries no as-of date so it is cited as undated-current) x the PUBLISHED encoding ladder, not a flat '3 encodings x 4 MB'. Spotify's audio-quality support page lists ~24 / ~96 / ~160 / ~320 kbit/s in the apps plus AAC 128 (Free) and AAC 256 (Premium) on the web player: at a ~3.5-minute average track that is ~26 MB per track, ~2.6 PB - and 24-bit/44.1 kHz FLAC shipped 2025-09-10 (Spotify newsroom), adding roughly another ~33 MB per track wherever it is present. The previous 1.2 PB undercounted the ladder. STILL EXCLUDED, so 5 PB remains an undercount: podcasts, audiobooks, cover art, and the storage replication factor.

assumptions.subject: cdn
assumptions.statement: Delivery volume: ~512 kB per chunk at a ~128 kbit/s ladder average x the chunk rate. This volume is UNCHANGED from the previous 10-second/160 KB segment model, and that is the honest half of the chunk-size correction: bytes/s = listeners x bitrate is invariant of chunk size, so fixing the chunk size moved the REQUEST count and not one byte of egress. The same 128 kbit/s ladder average drives both the chunk cadence and the byte volume, so the two are internally consistent; assume the 160 kbit/s High tier instead and BOTH the request rate and the egress rise together.

assumptions.subject: pricing
assumptions.statement: Monthly usage volumes (egress/storage/requests) are derived from AVERAGE load = peak / 3; capacity and instance counts are sized to PEAK. A single system_rps cannot carry both, so the peak:average ratio is stated here rather than hidden in a volume.

assumptions.subject: pricing
assumptions.statement: Delivery egress is priced at the model's single flat internet-egress rate ($0.09/GB, the US first paid tier). At the petabyte-per-month volume this design implies, a real committed CDN contract is roughly 5-10x cheaper, so the egress line is an UPPER BOUND, not a quote. The volume (GB/month) is the engineering claim; the rate is not negotiated here. For a music service this line is the ENTIRE bill's shape: compute is under 1% of it. That conclusion is robust to the rate; the absolute figure is not. Note that with the catalogue corrected to ~5 PB, origin STORAGE is no longer a rounding error beside egress - read both lines from the engine's computed cost table, not from this note

assumptions.subject: scope
assumptions.statement: Personalised recommendations, home-shelf ML ranking, DRM key serving, offline sync and the ad platform are OUT of this reference. Query-driven SEARCH is IN: this file names search in a component, so it must model it honestly rather than affirmatively claim it and then hide it behind a scope line.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: Control-plane rates derive from the same ~160,000 listeners and did NOT change when the chunk size was corrected: ~1,000 playback starts/s (one start per listener per ~160 s, i.e. a ~3.5-minute track with skipping, consistent with the measured 'Approximately 39% of playbacks in Spotify are by random access', Kreitz & Niemela, IEEE P2P'10), ~2 browse/search actions per play, plus a resume/progress heartbeat and library writes. Only the SHARES were re-derived, because the audio flow shrank by ~3.2x.

assumptions.subject: search
assumptions.statement: Search is a DEDICATED RETRIEVAL TIER, not a SQL read replica. Spotify: 'Search at Spotify relied mostly on term matching' via 'our Elasticsearch cluster', with dense Natural Language Search added 'as an additional source', plus 'a final-stage reranking model that takes the top candidates from each retrieval source' (Spotify Engineering, 2022-03-17). SCOPE CAVEAT, stated because it matters: that post is about PODCAST EPISODE search. It evidences Spotify's retrieval architecture; it is NOT evidence that music catalogue search is identical. ~35% of browse/search actions are assumed to reach this tier as an actual query - no public figure exists for that split either - and the rest are shelf, playlist and library browsing served from cache.

assumptions.subject: search
assumptions.statement: Search tier capacity is ASSUMED at 300 rps per instance over 3 instances, at ~45 ms of service time. NO Spotify, Elasticsearch or vendor figure is cited for either - this is reasoned from the SHAPE of the work and is the first number a reader should challenge. It is deliberately and materially below the 8,000 rps this file assumes for a SQL point-read replica, because a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank pipeline SCORES candidates with a model instead of fetching one keyed row. The teaching point is the order-of-magnitude gap between ranked retrieval and a point read, not the digit.

assumptions.subject: search
assumptions.statement: GAP - the search tier is priced as a CPU app server (m6i.large, copied from the same-kind app_server rows already priced in this file) because that is the only same-kind price this file carries evidence for. A real final-stage neural reranker is commonly served on accelerators whose cost this model does NOT carry, so the search line is a FLOOR. GAP also: the catalogue metadata store that feeds the index is not modelled as its own component - the index is treated as self-contained. At Spotify that store is not a SQL replica either: 'petabytes reside in Bigtable for online use-cases' (Spotify Engineering, 2026-07-27).

assumptions.subject: replica
assumptions.statement: The read replicas now serve ONLY keyed account, entitlement and playlist reads, and they will read as nearly idle. That is the lesson, not an oversight: a keyed point read scales trivially, ranked retrieval does not. This component was previously called 'Read replicas (catalogue browse, search backing)' with catalogue search routed onto it, which taught a reader that catalogue search scales by adding PostgreSQL read replicas and would never be their constraint. It does not, and it is.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Spotify ran exactly this shape and outgrew it: 'Reads were distributed over all data centers, but writes only took place in London. On a single machine.' - and the final cut-over to Cassandra 'was made on May 11th' 2015, because that single writer was both a scaling ceiling and a single point of failure (Spotify Engineering, 2015-06, 'Switching user database on a running system'). A reader copying this reference should treat the single writer as a stage to grow out of, not a destination.

assumptions.subject: store
assumptions.statement: Object-store base latency is 50 ms with a 30-100 ms band - the ONE latency in this file a Spotify primary can grade: 'GCS delivers 30-100ms per request' (Spotify Engineering, 2026-07-27). It was previously 20 ms, which is faster than the modelled company's own published figure for that storage class. Every other latency here (CDN, LB, cache, DB, replica, search) has NO public Spotify figure behind it and remains an assumption.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: GAP - the client-side cache is not modelled at all. The ~160,000 concurrent listeners are inferred from SERVER request rate, and Kreitz & Niemela measured that only '8.8% of data came from servers, 35.8% from the peer-to-peer network, and the remaining 55.4% were cached data' (IEEE P2P'10). The P2P overlay was retired in 2014; the local cache and prefetch were not - clients 'start downloading the next track when 30 seconds or less remain of the current track'. So 160,000 is a LOWER BOUND on real concurrent listeners: the model errs in the SAFE direction for capacity and UNDERSTATES the user base this design implies. Independent corroboration of the chunk size from the same paper: clients 'normally make between zero and ten server requests for a track', 'the mean size being 440 kB' - close to the modern 512 kB chunk.

_library.summary: Chunked range-request audio streaming with a CDN-dominated delivery path, a dedicated search-retrieval tier as the control-plane constraint, and a play-event pipeline.
